fact: Aubrey Lee Price wrote an unpublished memoir titled The Inglorious Fugitive, from the preface of which he describes sitting on a rock near a foreign border, covered in sweat, blood, and dirt.
The last memory Hannah Price has of her father before he vanished is waking up to him praying over her.
Aubrey Lee Price was known to everyone as Lee Price, not Aubrey.
In the late 1990s Lee Price was a pastor at a small Baptist church in Griffin, Georgia.
Lee Price also served as pastor at Clear Springs Baptist Church in Johns Creek.
Lee Price led mission trips to South America to build churches and distribute clothes to the poor.
Lee Price ran his own multimillion-dollar investment firm called PFG for four years before his disappearance.
More than a hundred of Price's clients, many of whom had come through his church, entrusted him with their life savings.
Price's most expensive purchase was a five-bedroom home in Bradenton, Florida, with a heated pool, just a short walk from Sarasota Bay.
Price remodeled the Bradenton home with a friend and did the landscaping himself.
Price sold the family home in Florida and moved to Valdosta, to a house half the size and a third the price.
Eighteen months before Price's disappearance, his firm had taken a controlling stake in Montgomery Bank & Trust, located in tiny Ailey, Georgia, halfway between Savannah and Macon.
Hannah Price was seventeen years old on the morning her father stood over her weeping before he vanished.
On the evening of June 16, 2012, Lee Price boarded a ferry from Key West to Fort Myers wearing khaki shorts and a white shirt.
Price threw his small carry-on suitcase overboard along with his cell phone from the ferry, keeping only a backpack with diving weights and his driver's license.
Price wrote in chapter four of The Inglorious Fugitive that he planned to jump from the third-floor deck of the ferry and die at the Estero River, one of his favorite places from childhood.
Charles Bethea met with Lee Price over four visits in February and March at the Bulloch County Jail in Statesboro, talking for ten hours total.
Lee Price gave Bethea a copy of the first eight chapters of The Inglorious Fugitive at their third meeting.
Lee Price is being held at the Bulloch County Jail in Statesboro until his trial on federal charges of bank fraud related to the failing of Montgomery Bank & Trust in 2012.
Federal prosecutors in New York also indicted Price on wire and securities fraud charges.
Lee Price became one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives, with a $20,000 reward offered for information leading to his capture.
Price reappeared on New Year's Eve after a routine traffic stop in Glynn County, eighteen months after he led everyone to believe he was on his way to die.
When Price made his first appearance before a judge on January 2, he had lost weight, let his hair grow long, and sported a beard, dyeing both black.
In 1976, a former Marine named Jim Price moved his young family from Atlanta to Florida's Palm Beach County, where they farmed squash and eggplant.
Jim Price told Bethea that his son Lee "picked vegetables all day long" and "never complained" at age ten.
Lee Price's eleventh-grade chemistry teacher and tennis coach, Victor Wolfe, admired Lee enough to name a child after him.
Victor Wolfe said of Lee Price, He was never cocky. Very coachable. He had a good head on his shoulders. He was sensitive and hard-working.
Beginning in 1987, Lee Price became deeply involved in church and worked at a power plant for two years to earn money for college.
Lee Price attended Brewton-Parker, a Baptist college in Mount Vernon, Georgia, where he met his wife, Rebekah, and graduated in 1990 with a bachelor's in ministry.
Price pursued a master's degree from Columbia International University before taking his first head minister job in Pelion, South Carolina, where his first two children, Nathan and Hannah, were born.
Gail Cantrell, Teamon's financial secretary, said of Price, He's the best preacher I've ever worked under. And he set a great example. My daughter is a missionary because of him.
Price directed that his $30,000 salary as pastor at Clear Springs Baptist Church go toward mission work, specifically to Global Discipleship, his charity in Venezuela.
Paris Stone, financial director at Clear Springs and Price's client for years, confirmed that Price's entire salary "went to Global Discipleship, his charity in Venezuela."
In 2000 Price moved the family to Alpharetta and went to work for the brokerage firm Salomon Smith Barney, with his new office off I-285 near Peachtree Dunwoody Road.
In 2003 Price left Smith Barney for Banc of America Securities, after which his investor list ballooned to 500.
Price started PFG in January of 2008, a little over a year after obtaining his Series 24 broker license.
Price's son Nathan told Bethea, He's my hero. My favorite thing to do was watch my dad preach. I would just blow up with pride.
Price drove the same old truck, a 2001 Dodge Durango, for years.

Since its inception, PFG had raised $40 million from investors, $36.9 million of which went into a trading account at Goldman Sachs; when the account was closed in mid-May of 2012, only $480,000 was left.
The night before Price left for good, he watched Braveheart with his oldest son Nathan, and they stayed up late talking about church, the ministry, and where Nathan was heading in life.
Price's last words to Nathan in person were, "Never give up. Never give up."
Security cameras show Price wearing khaki shorts, sneakers, a white long-sleeve shirt, and a red cap while exiting the Key West airport terminal on June 16, 2012.
Hannah Price said of her father, "He was my best friend," and described walking around the house crying after his disappearance.
Four months after Price's disappearance, Rebekah Price filed papers to have her husband declared deceased.

On December 31, 2012, a judge in Florida declared Aubrey Lee Price dead, and less than a month later one life insurance provider issued a check for $1.25 million, which eventually went into the receiver's asset pool.

Federal prosecutors said Aubrey Lee Price embezzled over $21 million from Montgomery Bank & Trust, and the later sentencing record described his fraud loss figure at $45,939,944.39 before it was reduced to $42,837,800.77 in the judgment, with the $21 million figure reflecting money taken from the bank rather than the full investor-and-bank loss total.

The federal court sentenced Aubrey Lee Price to 30 years in prison, followed by five years of supervised release, and ordered a $51 million forfeiture money judgment; restitution was to be determined later at a hearing.

Price was named a director of Montgomery Bank & Trust and, according to federal authorities, that role let him oversee the bank’s investments and gain access to more than $21 million, which he then moved into securities accounts and lost through risky trading.

Price sent a 22-page letter in June 2012 titled "Confidential Confession for Regulators" to acquaintances/individuals, and in it he wrote that he had "falsified statements with false returns" to conceal investor losses and that he blamed no one but himself.

Federal authorities said Price had "gained access to more than $21 million and lost more than $16 million through risky investments—all the while telling the bank the money was being used to purchase securities."

In a June 2012 22-page letter titled Confidential Confession For Regulators – PFG, LLC and PFGBI, LLC Summary, Price said he "falsified statements with false returns" to conceal between $20 million and $23 million in investor losses.

The FBI said Price’s mid-June 2012 "suicide letters" admitted he had defrauded MB&T Bank and his PFG investors and suggested he planned to kill himself by throwing himself off a high-speed ferry boat after it left the coast of Florida.
Price raised approximately $51 million from approximately 115 investors across the country in two investment funds he managed, PFG LLC and the Montgomery Growth Fund.
Price embezzled over $21 million in capital from Montgomery Bank & Trust over the next eighteen months.

Prosecutors said Aubrey Lee Price embezzled over $21 million from Montgomery Bank & Trust, while other filings and reports said his fraud consumed most of the roughly $40 million he raised from 115 clients and concealed about $20 million to $23 million in investor losses.
Price pleaded guilty to bank, wire, and securities fraud and was sentenced to 30 years in prison, with a plea deal calling for up to 30 years plus restitution that was reported as $51 million.
A contemporaneous SEC filing said Price’s June 2012 letter admitted he "falsified statements with false returns" to conceal between $20 million and $23 million in investor losses.
Prosecutors said Price misspent, embezzled and lost $21 million belonging to Montgomery Bank & Trust, and the FBI said his fraud exposed victims to millions of dollars in losses.
Price was sentenced to 70 years in prison, with the sentences to run concurrently, and was expected to pay about $46 million in restitution.

In mid-June 2012, Aubrey Lee Price sent “suicide letters” admitting he had defrauded MB&T Bank and PFG investors, and on December 31, 2013 he was arrested after presenting false identification during a routine traffic stop in Brunswick, Georgia.

The SEC complaint says Price’s scheme involved an ongoing fraud in two funds and that he admitted in a June 2012 confession letter he had “falsified statements with false returns” to conceal between $20 million and $23 million in investor losses.
The SEC complaint identifies Price’s funds as PFG LLC and PFGBI, LLC and says the June 2012 letter was titled “Confidential Confession For Regulators – PFG, LLC and PFGBI, LLC Summary.”

The case worked through investment-fund and bank-fraud mechanics: according to the SEC, Price used fabricated statements with false returns to conceal losses in the funds, while the DOJ said he also falsified documents showing about $17 million on deposit at a major New York financial firm to hide MB&T losses.
The DOJ said Price defrauded dozens of investors and a federally insured bank, and the SEC complaint says the scheme concealed between $20 million and $23 million in losses.
According to the FDIC complaint, Price misappropriated $14,700,000 from MBT between January 2011 and May 2012.

The FBI called Price “The Fraudster Who Faked His Own Death,” and the SEC said his June 2012 confession letter admitted falsifying returns to conceal losses, underscoring the scale and deception of the scheme.
Price was ordered to forfeit a total of $51 million, representing the proceeds of his crimes.
Price embezzled over $21 million in capital from MB&T (a federally insured bank).
Between June 2009 and June 2012, Price defrauded approximately 115 individual investors.
The 115 individual investors had invested $51 million in two investment funds managed by Price.
Price lost almost all of the $51 million from individual investors through speculative trading.
The total losses to investors and the bank exceeded $70 million.
Price managed two investment funds from which he defrauded the 115 individual investors.
The record describes Aubrey Lee Price as a former preacher and investment adviser before he founded PFG LLC and later served as a bank director with access to Montgomery Bank & Trust.

At the Brunswick, Georgia checkpoint, Price was stopped in a vehicle and identified by officers after giving his name; contemporaneous reports said he appeared as a fugitive banker who had faked his death and was taken into custody by local police and federal agents.

Some restitution details were still unresolved at sentencing and that the full disposition of investor claims remained tied to later proceedings, while civil and administrative matters continued in SEC and related litigation.

Price graduated from Brewton-Parker College in 1990 with a bachelor’s in ministry, worked at a power plant for two years, served as a Baptist pastor in Griffin and Johns Creek, and led mission trips to South America.
Price became a director of Montgomery Bank & Trust in December 2010 after a company he controlled bought a controlling stake, giving him access to oversee the bank’s investments.
The FBI later said Price went from a trusted financial adviser to a schemer who wiped out clients’ life savings and then faked his own death to avoid responsibility.
Price was arrested on December 31, 2013, after he presented false identification during a routine traffic stop in Brunswick, Georgia.

Price was described as a former preacher and investment adviser who created PFG LLC, and later admitted he had defrauded investors and regulators while also losing money through Montgomery Bank & Trust's securities portfolio.
Price became a director of Montgomery Bank & Trust in December 2010 when a company he controlled bought a controlling portion of the bank's stock, giving him influence over the bank's investments.
Federal authorities said Price 'stole, misappropriated and embezzled' money from the bank after being named a director and asked to oversee its investments.
